definitions.text: Classification is the process in which organisms are divided into groups and subgroups on the basis of similarities and differences found in them.
The groups into which organisms are classified are known as taxonomic ranks or taxa (singular “taxon”).
The highest taxonomic rank is domain. All organisms are divided into three domains: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya.
Domain is further divided into kingdoms. For example, the domain Eukarya is divided into four kingdoms i.e., Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista.
Each kingdom is subdivided into related phyla or divisions.
Each phylum/division is divided into related classes.
Each class is further divided into related orders.
Each order is broken down into related families.
Each family is divided into related genera (singular genus).
It is the lowest level of classification. A species is a group of similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile (capable of reproduction) offspring.
The system of scientific naming of organisms is termed as binomial nomenclature.
For scientific naming, words are taken from Latin language.
Every scientific name has two parts. The genus name always comes first followed by the species name.
Every scientific name should have to be unique because the same name cannot be used for naming two different organisms.
The first part of the name i.e. genus name should begin with a capital letter. The second part of the name i.e. species name should begin with small letter.
At the time of printing of a scientific name, it should be typed in Italics.
When a scientific name would be hand written, two parts of it should be separately underlined.

fullMarks: For a question about the Linnaean hierarchy, write the ranks in order from broadest to narrowest: domain, kingdom, phylum (division for plants and fungi), class, order, family, genus, species. If asked for the seven Linnaean ranks, leave out domain.

For a classification comparison, use clear headings such as cell type, cell wall, habitat and nutrition. State the key difference directly: archaea lack peptidoglycan in their cell walls, while bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan.
For a question on Eukarya, name all four kingdoms first—Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia—then give each kingdom’s defining cell type, nutrition and cell-wall features.

For virus questions, include the points that viruses are acellular, contain DNA or RNA surrounded by a protein coat, cannot run metabolism, and are not included in the classification system because they lack characteristics of the three domains.

For binomial-naming questions, state all relevant rules and give a correctly formatted example, such as *Homo sapiens*: genus first and capitalised, species second and lowercase, with both words italicised in print or separately underlined when handwritten.
Use scientific names accurately: write both parts, keep their order, and do not capitalise the species name. Label every rank clearly if you draw or complete a hierarchy.
mistakes: Mistake: Giving the seven Linnaean ranks but adding domain as one of the seven. Fix: The seven are kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species; domain was added later above kingdom.
Mistake: Saying bacterial cell walls contain no peptidoglycan. Fix: Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan; archaean cell walls do not contain peptidoglycan.
Mistake: Describing fungi as autotrophs or saying they ingest food. Fix: Fungi are heterotrophs that absorb food from their surroundings.
Mistake: Saying all protists are unicellular. Fix: Protists can be unicellular, colonial, filamentous or simple multicellular.

Mistake: Putting viruses in one of the three domains because they infect living things. Fix: State that viruses are acellular and are not included in the classification system because they lack characteristics of the three domains.

Mistake: Writing both words of a scientific name with capital letters, or writing the name as one word. Fix: Write the genus first with a capital letter and the species second with a lowercase letter; italicise both words in print or underline them separately by hand.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.3: What are the seven taxonomic ranks used in the Linnaean system?
shortTheory.answer: In this system, Linnaeus suggested seven taxonomic ranks i.e., kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family, genus and species.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.5: What are the basic differences between archaea and bacteria?
shortTheory.answer: Their cell wall does not contain peptidoglycan but is made of various polypeptides and proteins. Their rRNA (ribosomal RNA) resembles more to eukaryotes than to bacteria. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.6: What are the shortcomings of the three-kingdom classification system?
shortTheory.answer: In this system, fungi were still included in the kingdom Plantae. Some taxonomists disagreed about the position of fungi in kingdom Plantae. Fungi resemble plants in many ways but are heterotrophs which get their food by absorption. They do not have cellulose in their cell walls but possess chitin.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.7: Which kingdom includes organisms that are multicellular and heterotrophic, and lack cell walls?
shortTheory.answer: This kingdom includes animals which are eukaryotic, multicellular and heterotrophic.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.8: Enlist the distinguishing characteristics of fungi.
shortTheory.answer: They are heterotrophic. Fungi get nutrients in a unique way. They do not ingest food like animals and some protists. They absorb food from decaying matter present in their surroundings. Fungi are eukaryotic and have cell wall around their cells. Their cell wall is made of chitin (a polysaccharide).

shortTheory.question: Short 2.9: List the three domains that encompass all living organisms.
shortTheory.answer: Living organisms are broadly classified into three domains: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.10: Why cannot we classify viruses in any kingdom?
shortTheory.answer: Viruses are not included in the classification system because they lack any of the characteristics of the three domains of life.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.11: How does binomial nomenclature facilitate clear communication about organisms across different languages?
shortTheory.answer: The scientific name of an organism is same anywhere in the world. This system provides a standard way of communication, whether the language of a particular biologist is Chinese, Arabic, Spanish, or English.
